title: Kingdoms Plantae and Animalia
summary: Plantae are multicellular, eukaryotic autotrophs with cellulosic cell walls, all embryophytes. Divisions: Bryophyta (non-vascular), Pteridophyta (vascular, no seeds) and Spermatophyta (seed plants), the last being divided into Gymnospermae (naked seeds) and Angiospermae (seeds enclosed in the ovary; dicotyledons and monocotyledons).

Bryophyta are the amphibians of the plant kingdom; they have no xylem or phloem and no true roots, stems or leaves; the main plant body is the haploid gametophyte, attached by rhizoids; the sex organs are antheridia (male) and archegonia (female), both jacketed; the sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte and produces spores by meiosis. Types: liverworts (Marchantia), mosses (Funaria) and hornworts (Anthoceros). The life cycle shows alternation of generations. Bryophytes are pioneers of vegetation, soil binders and hold water. Pteridophyta (ferns) are lower vascular plants whose main plant body is the diploid sporophyte with rhizome, roots and fronds (leaves with rachis, pinnae and pinnules, young leaves circinately coiled); sporangia are in groups called sori (covered by indusium); spores grow into a free-living prothallus (gametophyte) bearing antheridia and archegonia.

Gymnosperms (Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus, Sequoia, Juniperus) bear naked ovules on ovuliferous scales in cones; plants are tall, woody and evergreen; vascular bundles in a ring with secondary growth; Pinus has winged pollen grains and dimorphic leaves; products: timber, resin, turpentine, chilgoza and sago from Cycas. Angiosperms: seeds enclosed in fruit (a mature ovary). Differences from gymnosperms: seeds enclosed versus naked; flowers versus cones; vessels present in angiosperm xylem (absent in gymnosperms). Dicots have two cotyledons, reticulate venation, tap root, pentamerous (4 or 5) flowers and collateral open bundles in a ring; monocots have one cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots, trimerous flowers and scattered closed bundles.

Families: Fabaceae (pea): zygomorphic, bisexual flowers; five sepals; five petals (standard, two wings, two keel petals, papilionaceous); ten stamens in two bundles (9+1, diadelphous); superior monocarpellary ovary with marginal placentation; fruit a pod; e.g. Pisum sativum, Cajanus cajan, Arachis hypogaea. Malvaceae (china rose): actinomorphic, pentamerous flowers with epicalyx; five sepals and petals; indefinite stamens joined in a staminal tube (monadelphous); five syncarpous carpels with axile placentation; fruit capsule; e.g. Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, cotton, bhindi. Liliaceae (lily; monocot): perennial herbs with bulbs or rhizomes; trimerous, actinomorphic, hypogynous flowers; six petaloid perianth lobes; six stamens; three syncarpous carpels; fruit capsule; e.g. Allium cepa, Aloe, Asparagus. Poaceae (grass; monocot): inflorescence of spikelets; three stamens; unilocular ovary with a single basal ovule; fruit caryopsis; e.g. Oryza sativa, Triticum aestivum, Zea mays, sugarcane.

Animals are multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic with ingestive nutrition, locomotion and a nervous system. Basis of classification: level of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ-system), symmetry (asymmetrical, radial, bilateral), body cavity (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, eucoelomate), embryonic layers (diploblastic, triploblastic) and the notochord (chordates versus non-chordates).

Porifera (sponges): pores, canal system, osculum, spongocoel, spicules, asymmetrical, marine. Cnidaria (Hydra, jellyfish, corals): radial, diploblastic, cnidoblasts (stinging cells), polyp and medusa forms. Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorsoventrally flattened, acoelomate, single opening of gut (none in tapeworm), mostly parasitic (Fasciola, Taenia); Planaria is free living. Aschelminthes (roundworms): cylindrical, pseudocoelomate, complete gut, separate sexes (Ascaris, Wuchereria). Annelida: segmented, coelomate, setae or parapodia, nephridia (earthworm Pheretima, Nereis, leech Hirudinaria). Arthropoda: jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, head, thorax and abdomen; classes Arachnida (4 pairs of legs, scorpion), Crustacea (prawn), Myriapoda (centipede, millipede) and Insecta (3 pairs of legs, cockroach). Mollusca: soft unsegmented body, shell, muscular foot (snail, octopus). Echinodermata: marine, radial symmetry, water vascular system with tube feet (starfish, sea urchin).

Chordata: notochord, dorsal tubular nerve cord and gill slits at some stage. Subphyla: Urochordata (Herdmania), Cephalochordata (Amphioxus) and Vertebrata. Agnatha (jawless; Cyclostomata, Petromyzon) and Gnathostomata (jawed): Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fish, e.g. dogfish Scoliodon, ventral mouth, no operculum), Osteichthyes (bony fish, e.g. Labeo, operculum), Amphibia (three-chambered heart, moist skin, tympanum, e.g. frog, toad), Reptilia (dry scaly skin, three-chambered heart with partial ventricle division, four-chambered in crocodiles, leathery eggs, no hair), Aves (feathers, beak, pneumatic bones, four-chambered heart, syrinx, only left ovary, forelimbs as wings), Mammalia (hair, mammary glands, pinna, four-chambered heart, thecodont and heterodont teeth, diaphragm, viviparous).
mcq: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of flatworms (Platyhelminthes)?
Which of them is a true fish?
Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because —
The dominant phase of a fern is —
The stamens of the pea flower are —
The excretory organs of earthworm are —
The class of animals with a four-chambered heart and pneumatic bones is —
Tube feet are the organs of locomotion in —
Which of the following is a cartilaginous fish?
Which of the following is a pseudocoelomate?
objective: Match: (a) Malvaceae (b) Fabaceae (c) Poaceae with (i) Pisum sativum (ii) Hibiscus rosa-sinensis (iii) Oryza sativa.
Fill in the blanks: (a) The male sex organ of bryophytes is the ______. (b) The spore-bearing structures of a fern occur in groups called ______.
State true or false: (a) Gymnosperms have seeds enclosed in an ovary. (b) The fern prothallus is a gametophyte.
(a) False – the seeds are naked. (b) True.
Name the phylum: (a) tube feet (b) cnidoblasts.
Give the number of stamens in: (a) Fabaceae (b) Liliaceae.
Give the botanical name of (a) rice (b) wheat.
Name one example each: (a) liverwort (b) moss.
Give the number of heart chambers in (a) a frog (b) a crocodile.
vsa: With reference to class Reptilia, identify the two wrong statements: (a) Body is covered by hairs (b) Paired pentadactyl limbs with clawed digits (c) Respiration by lungs (d) Heart is two chambered.
(a) and (d) are wrong. The body of reptiles is covered by dry horny scales, not hair, and the heart is three-chambered (four-chambered in crocodiles), not two-chambered.
With the help of suitable diagrams differentiate between the androecium in pea and china rose.
Pea (Fabaceae): 10 stamens, diadelphous (9 fused in one bundle and 1 free). China rose (Malvaceae): numerous stamens fused by their filaments into a staminal tube (monadelphous).
Write two differences between gymnosperms and angiosperms.
Gymnosperm seeds are naked (borne on cones) and xylem lacks vessels; angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits and xylem has vessels.
Write any two general characters of phylum Arthropoda.
Jointed legs and a chitinous exoskeleton, with a segmented body divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
Why are sponges classed as the lowest animals?
They are asymmetrical, have a cellular grade of organisation without tissues or organs, and have a canal system.
List two economic importance of gymnosperms.
They yield timber and resins or turpentine; chilgoza (dry fruit) and sago from Cycas.
Distinguish between cartilaginous and bony fishes (any two points).
Cartilaginous fishes (Scoliodon) have a cartilaginous skeleton, ventral mouth and no operculum; bony fishes (Labeo) have a bony skeleton, terminal mouth and an operculum.
Name the two subkingdoms of Animalia and give their basis.
Parazoa (no tissues, cellular grade, e.g. sponges) and Eumetazoa (tissue or organ grades of organisation).
sa: Write the characteristic features of Bryophyta.

They are non-vascular embryophytes; the independent plant body is the haploid gametophyte; it has rhizoids but no true roots, stems or leaves; sex organs are antheridia and archegonia surrounded by a sterile jacket; the dependent sporophyte produces spores by meiosis.
Describe the main features of the family Fabaceae.

Zygomorphic, bisexual flowers; five sepals; five papilionaceous petals (standard, two wings and two keel petals); ten diadelphous stamens; monocarpellary superior ovary with marginal placentation; the fruit is a pod; examples are pea and gram.
Give the main characteristics of the family Malvaceae.

Actinomorphic pentamerous flowers with an epicalyx; five free petals; numerous monadelphous stamens joined into a staminal tube; five syncarpous carpels with axile placentation; fruit a capsule; e.g. Hibiscus, cotton, bhindi.
They are warm-blooded with feathers, a beak without teeth, pneumatic bones, forelimbs modified into wings, a four-chambered heart, a syrinx and only the left ovary, and they lay shelled eggs.
Write any three characters of Phylum Platyhelminthes with examples.
Dorsoventrally flattened and acoelomate, with a gut that has a single opening or is absent; mostly parasitic; examples are Planaria, Fasciola and Taenia.
List the distinguishing features of Mammalia.
Hair on the body, mammary glands, external ears (pinnae), heterodont and thecodont dentition, four-chambered heart, diaphragm and viviparity.
la: Classify the Kingdom Plantae into divisions with their main characteristics.

Bryophyta: non-vascular, gametophyte dominant. Pteridophyta: vascular, sporophyte dominant, spores in sori. Spermatophyta: seed plants, divided into gymnosperms (naked seeds, cones) and angiosperms (seeds in fruits; dicots with two cotyledons and monocots with one).

Seed with two versus one cotyledon; tap root versus fibrous root; reticulate versus parallel venation; flowers pentamerous versus trimerous; vascular bundles in a ring, open and collateral versus scattered and closed.
Classify phylum Arthropoda into classes with examples.

Arachnida (cephalothorax, four pairs of legs; scorpion), Crustacea (cephalothorax with carapace; prawn), Myriapoda (many segments with 1-2 pairs of legs each; centipede, millipede) and Insecta (head, thorax with three pairs of legs and wings, abdomen; cockroach).
Describe the characteristic features of the classes Amphibia and Reptilia.

Amphibia: live on land and in water, moist glandular skin, no claws, three-chambered heart, eggs laid in water, gills in larva and lungs in adult (frog). Reptilia: dry scaly skin, clawed digits, lungs, three-chambered heart with a partial septum (four in crocodile), leathery shelled eggs on land (lizard, snake).
Describe the basis for the classification of animals.
Level of organisation, symmetry, body cavity, number of germ layers and presence of the notochord, with examples of each category.
